title: Read, experiment, and comment on How AI reduces the world to stereotypes
creators_list: Anna Mills (College of Marin)
description: This assignment guides students in analyzing algorithmic bias through a combination of critical reading and practical experimentation. Students first annotate the article "How AI reduces the world to stereotypes" by Victoria Turk using Perusall, identifying claims and nuances in the argument. The core activity requires students to use AI tools (such as Dall-E or Stable Diffusion) to generate images of specific identities. They then analyze these outputs for inherent biases, assumptions, or inaccuracies and share their findings. By discussing both the text and their generated images with peers, students practice "slow thinking" regarding AI ethics and prepare for future argumentative writing. This resource effectively blends theoretical analysis with a hands-on audit of generative AI tools.

title: AI Bias Tutorial and Hands-On Activity
creators_list: Nick Szydlowski (San José State University)
description: This web-based tutorial introduces the concept of bias in artificial intelligence (AI) systems and provides learners with a hands-on activity for exploring the potential for bias in AI systems. The tutorial first introduces the concept of AI bias through the work of Dr. Joy Buolamwini, which focuses on bias in facial recognition algorithms. The hands-on portion of the tutorial focuses on bias in chatbots based on large language models (LLMs). Using a custom chat tool, participants are encouraged to reproduce methods from peer-reviewed research on gender bias in LLMs, and to try their own prompts to explore ways of detecting bias in LLMs. The tool sends the same prompt to Google Gemini ten times, allowing users to see variation in chatbot responses due to the intentional randomness that is a feature of those systems, and to validate their own observations of bias by seeing the recurrence of biased responses over multiple responses.

title: Bias and Influence in Search Tools
creators_list: Melody Chin (Singapore Management University)
description: This module introduces students to how internet search tools shape what we see, and what we miss, when we look for information online. It explains in accessible terms how search engines collect data, rank results, and personalize what different users see on the same query. Learners explore examples of bias in search results, including commercial influence, default settings, and culturally skewed content. The module highlights how these invisible choices can reinforce stereotypes or marginalize some perspectives while amplifying others. Throughout, students are prompted to think critically about why particular results appear first and how design features like snippets and sponsored links affect their decisions. It concludes with practical strategies for reducing bias in their own searching, such as comparing tools, adjusting settings, and diversifying keywords, so that they can become more reflective, responsible, and effective searchers in academic and everyday contexts. Self-check questions reinforce understanding and support independent, flexible learning.

title: Assessing fair AI use: Rubric development for assessing ethical and social equity concerns in AI
creators_list: Sarah Tribelhorn (San Diego State University)
description: In Activity 1 (“The AI Audit”), students enact Authority Is Constructed and Contextual by interrogating who/what confers credibility on AI outputs and how opacity in training data limits authority claims. Using the rubric to probe Fairness/Bias, Transparency, and Accountability also operationalizes Research as Inquiry. The live demo and small-group investigations practice Searching as Strategic Exploration, while the brief report-out positions learners within Scholarship as Conversation as they share findings and challenge assumptions together. Activity 2 (“Uncovering the Planetary Costs”) extends Information Creation as a Process by mapping the sociotechnical systems behind AI, including data centers, energy/water use, mining, logistics, and makes explicit that Information Has Value (economic, environmental, and human). Collectively, the activities yield measurable outcomes: students can articulate criteria for AI credibility; identify gaps in transparency; describe environmental and social impacts with citations; and propose responsible, equitable practices for using generative tools.

title: Writing and Artificial Intelligence & Teaching and Artificial Intelligence
creators_list: Liza Long (College of Western Idaho), Joel Gladd (College of Western Idaho)
description: Section II," Writing and Artificial Intelligence," addresses some of the foundational basics regarding AI and its relation to academic writing. This section takes a “deliberate and critical approach to generative AI” to encourage students to “slow down and consider new tools critically” (https://idaho.pressbooks.pub/write/part/writing-and-artificial-intelligence/). It does not propose to students how they “should” or “should not” use AI tools in their writing assignments, but rather asks them to reflect and think critically about the benefits and drawbacks of doing so. It presents different scenarios where AI might be useful, and that they can think through as examples, and it emphasizes the importance of ethical considerations and only using AI in ways that are endorsed by their instructors and course policies. There is attention to ethical considerations, understanding syllabus policies, and even identifying their own AI adoption style as either “centaurs,” “cyborgs,” or “resisters.” In other words, it asks students to self-reflect and examine how they think about and interact with AI in the way that they do.

title: Building Ethical AI Literacy Across the First-Year Writing Sequence
creators_list: Russell Michalak (Goldey-Beacom College)
description: This collection of four Teaching and Learning Objects (TLOs) by Russell Michalak integrates critical AI literacy into the first-year college writing curriculum at an Emerging Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI) that primarily serves first-generation, low-socioeconomic, and multilingual students. Spanning two semesters, this instructional sequence utilizes equitable access to institutionally-licensed AI tools, including Grammarly, Scholarcy, Litmaps, and ImageFX, within a supportive library-based classroom staffed by faculty, librarians, and peer tutors. Students engage in scaffolded assignments ranging from narrative revisions and analytical responses to multimodal visual expressions and scholarly network mapping. Crucially, AI utilization remains entirely optional; parallel traditional activities like peer revision and manual database searches are provided. However, rigorous critical reflection regarding algorithmic bias, authorship, and cultural representation is mandatory for everyone. Together, these TLOs scaffold writing, critical evaluation, and visual literacy across two semesters, fostering ethical awareness, critical thinking, and digital fluency while amplifying the voices of first-generation, multilingual, and underrepresented learners.

title: Can AI Be a Co-Author?: How Generative AI Challenges the Boundaries of Authorship in a General Education Writing Class
creators_list: Holly Ryan (Penn State Berks), Daniel Abramov, Samantha Acker, Sydney Elkins
description: Published in Thresholds in Education, this collaborative article by Associate Professor Holly Ryan and three of her students explores the emerging role of GenAI in the composition classroom. Ryan details an instructional assignment sequence where honors English students wrote both about and with GenAI tools in order to evaluate their utility as co-authors. The authors examine the tools' strengths and weaknesses as co-authors and assess how effectively they contribute to the authoring process across various academic fields. Furthermore, the piece distinguishes between co-authorship as a final product versus as an experiential process, analyzing how GenAI fits into these dual frameworks. Ultimately, the article delves into student conclusions regarding human-AI collaborative writing and outlines four important components of human-AI collaborative writing that instructors can integrate into their own teaching to guide future classroom instructional practices.

description: "CAREful FAIRness in the Research Data Lifecycle" by Ateanna Uriri (Texas A&M University) is a curriculum introducing students to the Principles of Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics (CARE) and Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR), and how these principles apply to each stage of the research data lifecycle. Each session provides a short, accessible description of the purpose of a given stage, prompts students to consider how they will steward their datasets ethically, and offers resources to support their practice. The curriculum introduces or reinforces understanding of the FAIR Principles, commonly discussed in research data management, while highlighting the CARE Principles and their focus on the people, communities, and environments from which research data may originate. These principles encourage learners to "actively protect, nurture, and respect the environments and communities embedded within datasets" (Çay, Rodighiero & Zhang, 2025). The curriculum emphasizes that data are not isolated or context-free; they have histories and contexts that extend beyond individual research projects and must be considered throughout the research data lifecycle. Intended for undergraduate students and above, the curriculum's time requirements vary depending on how it is used.

title: Chaos Creator Game
creators_list: Mandi Goodsett (Cleveland State University)
description:
Combating the spread of misinformation is a struggle that has inspired considerable research in the fields of psychology, education, political science, and information science, among others. Such research has found that “prebunking” or “inoculation” techniques — strategies that reduce the acceptance of misinformation before one has encountered it — have had marked success. One of the most successful prebunking interventions is the game “Bad News,” developed by Roozenbeek and van der Linden (2019). In the game, participants try to gain as many followers as possible on their social media platform. To do this, players engage in the strategies of misinformation-creators: they fabricate information, sow doubt about credible public figures and organizations, and promote belief in conspiracy theories, all of which increases engagement with the players’ posts. In the process, participants learn how misinformation is created and how appealing it can be, which raises their skepticism and improves their ability to identify misinformation.
This game, called Chaos Creator, is a modified version of the Bad News game. It incorporates the prebunking strategies of raising skepticism by describing common misinformation persuasion tactics. Students play the game in-person during a library information literacy instruction one-shot session.

title: Using Collaborative and Creative Strategies to Personalize Media Literacy
creators_list: Amira Walker (Washington and Lee University)
description: This TLO is designed to help students enrolled in an introductory mass communications course to learn media literacy and develop the skills necessary to determine fact from fiction in the endless stream of information they encounter. The activity is a three-part process. It begins with a librarian guest lecture and workshop, where students learn the SIFT method for evaluating sources (Caulfield, 2019). Then, students complete a two-part assignment where they move beyond the evaluation process and engage in a collaborative group project, culminating in the creation of their own fake news story. Finally, students complete a written reflection, a metacognitive practice that gives them the opportunity to analyze the thought processes involved in spreading disinformation. The assignment includes elements of competition, interaction, creativity, source evaluation, and reflection. An important aspect of the assignment is that it includes significant student agency.  By incorporating student choice, the assignment acknowledges the expertise students bring to the classroom in terms of the platforms they use and the news topics that are trending and relevant to them.

title: Evaluating Online Information with SIFT
creators_list: Caitlin Benallack (Michigan State University)
description: This webpage moves students through the process of using SIFT, a strategy developed by Mike Caulfield, to evaluate online information. SIFT is made up of four “moves”: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, and trace the claims, quotes and media to the original context. The first part of the page introduces each of the four moves one at a time and pairs each move with a different real world source (tiktoks, tweets, news, and more) for students to practice the “move” on as a class. The second part of the page includes a downloadable worksheet and example sources that students can evaluate on their own or in small groups. This learning object was designed to be used with lower level undergraduate students preparing to do a project on a topic of their choice related to misinformation, conspiracies, and news literacy. The webpage was designed for a 90 minute face-to-face class session, but could easily be used in an online or asynchronous context.

title: The PBS NewsHour Classroom Media Literacy Survival Kit
creators_list: Kate Stevens (Poudre School District)
description: The PBS NewsHour Classroom Media Literacy Survival Kit is a hands-on lesson plan that helps middle and high school students become smarter consumers of online information. Students learn practical strategies to spot fake news, verify claims, and navigate social media misinformation by building their own digital detective toolkit. The main activity has students create a "survival kit" presentation featuring their chosen verification techniques. Working in pairs or small groups, they watch instructional videos, discuss real examples, and design creative materials showcasing the most important tips for checking online content. Students learn to pause when content triggers strong emotions, check multiple sources, look for credible evidence, and think critically before sharing information. The lesson includes ready-to-use materials like student guides, discussion prompts, and assessment rubrics that teachers can easily adapt for different class sizes and time constraints. Students practice concrete skills they can use immediately, such as reverse-searching images, identifying reliable sources, and recognizing common manipulation tactics. Rather than discouraging digital media use, this resource empowers students to engage more thoughtfully and safely with online information. Students develop practical verification habits they can apply to their daily social media interactions, making them more discerning consumers and sharers of digital content.

title: What Uses More? Compare the environmental footprint of digital tasks
creators_list: Jon Ippolito (What Uses More)
audience: high school; general public; educators; college; youth
description: This nonpartisan calculator is an attempt to provide a more objective comparison of the energy and water usage of various AI tasks versus other common digital activities, like watching Netflix or searching Google. The calculations are based on academic papers, industry reports, and expert estimates. The calculations include only current energy and water usage, and not growth scenarios or actual environmental impact. Even for energy and water, it's extremely difficult to do more than estimate values given the lack of transparency in the tech industry. It's also unclear how some future tradeoffs will play out, eg whether improved efficiencies will cancel out increased demand. These calculations also exclude numerous potential AI downsides apart from environmental risks, which you can find explained in the IMPACT RISK framework.
